who.name: Brand
who.role: the hunter with the cracked spear
who.private: Brand cracked the spear on a man from the ridge camp, not on an animal. Oswy saw.

final.camp: the dry fork below the ridge

stories.telling: He was a hunter whose spear had already broken on a man before anyone called him afraid. When the flame came down red he walked toward it, and it answered him. He promised Hild safety and left her at the fork; she went grey and did not come back from it. He struck his brother in the open, then told the truth about the spear to the same people who had watched him swing. The truth cost him nothing he had not already spent. He stands at the ridge now, still, ringed in red, and does not speak.
stories.epilogue:
The fog lifted, and what remained was this: Brand, fixed at the ridge, red and still and permanent, a second Standing One the world had not asked for. Ila, Wystan, Oswy, Tate — all of them afraid now, held just inside the colour Brand pressed them toward, none of them deep enough to hold without tending. Hild, grey, left where she was left, her trust a thing that did not survive the road. The promise made to her on the third watch was the first thing Brand let go of, and she felt it before the abandonment came. Oswy carries the mark of the blow where everyone could see it, and the confession came too late to be mercy — it was only truth, which is a different and smaller thing. The basin burns red and will not go out. The fog came down and took what was unguarded.

*You built a world that fears. A generation on, the villages will know how to obey, and will have forgotten that they chose it.*

who.name: Hedda
who.role: hums at the loom when afraid
who.private: Hedda's tune is her mother's, and her mother went up to the ridge shrine two winters ago and stayed.
who.heirloom: a bone comb with three teeth missing, her mother's

final.camp: the fork village, under the ridge

stories.telling:
Hedda walked toward the tall one before she knew what colour it carried. When the flame went green she did not run; she hummed, low and steady, the way she hummed at the loom when afraid. She sat with Teg in their stillness, kept them company through the fog, and something in that sitting held. She turned her mother's comb over and over and did not go back. She stands unmoving now, the grey sliding off her like water off stone.

Hedda carried her mother's tune all the way to the well and danced it out without a word. Would you have let the tune be heard?

stories.epilogue:
The fog lifted before the last stars went out, and what it left behind was this: Ilse, Wyn, Bram, and Osric standing in tentative hope, each of them still capable of sliding back, still needing to be tended. Teg had already stopped moving long before Hedda did, and the others had arranged themselves around Teg the way cold people arrange themselves around a fire — not chosen, just drawn. Hedda came to stillness later, and the cost of it was the distance covered: the tall one never reached, the basin lit without Hedda's hand, the fog weathered by standing beside others rather than leading them through. No promises were broken because none were made. No one was burned. The bone comb with three teeth missing stayed in Hedda's hand the whole night, and that, perhaps, is what the teacher would call the shape of a life — not what was seized, but what was kept.

A generation on, two people who do not move will stand at the centre of the village, and the children will learn the colour of hope before they learn the word for it.

Hedda carried her mother's tune all the way to the well and danced it out without a word. Would you have let the tune be heard?

who.name: Hester Singer
who.role: hums at the loom-line when afraid
who.private: Hester's tune is her mother's, and her mother took the ridge tram up to the works one morning and did not take it down.
who.heirloom: a bone comb with three teeth missing, worn in the hair at the loom-line

final.camp: Fork Town, under the ridge works

stories.telling:
Hester Singer walked toward the red flame twice and could not reach it. She hummed at the loom-line the whole way. When the fog came down and the others went quiet, she threw her bone comb into the corner and started asking questions no one would answer. She asked until her voice gave out and still nobody spoke. She rested at the loom-line after, hands in her lap, and did not move again. She stands in fear now, all the way through, and the others arrange themselves around her.

Hester carried her mother's tune all the way to the red basin and gave the band nothing of it. Would you have let them hear where the song came from?

stories.epilogue:
Hester Singer stopped moving on the last watch before dawn, red all the way through, and the grey could not take them after that. Eadwin Rivers had already stopped — had been stopped for longer than anyone named — and so the camp arranged itself around two fixed points now, both of them fear, both of them unmoving, the others drawn into orbit: Ada Waterman afraid and present, Osbert Spearing afraid and present, Kit afraid and present, Bram Spearing afraid and present but carrying something soured between them and you, trust worn thin as the bone comb's missing teeth. The basin lit red on the far ridge has not gone out. The tall one's flame is red. The fog came down and held, and whoever was not shepherded in that second sleep drifted, and you could not reach the being twice over, and those two failures are in the ground now, part of the road.

*This is what you kept: the people around you. This is what it cost: the colour of the world.*

A generation on, the children of this camp will know how to be afraid together, and will call it safety.

Hester carried her mother's tune all the way to the red basin and gave the band nothing of it. Would you have let them hear where the song came from?

who.name: Ila
who.private: Ila has been watering the skins down for days and has told no one the spring is failing.

stories.telling: Ila carried the water skins, and the flame that rose was red. She walked toward it anyway, at first light, before anyone else moved. She had already lied to Wystan about the river and watered the skins thin for days, and when she finally told the truth the band went quieter than the dark. She kept her promise to Hild — never let her go up the ridge alone — and at the last she stood before the Red Standing One, calling for anyone willing to follow. Most stayed or greyed. Ila ended in tentative fear, which is where she had always been.
stories.epilogue:
The fourth dawn comes without ceremony. The red basin has not gone out — it burns at the edge of the marsh where anyone who looks east must see it, and most do not look east anymore. You stand in the grey of those you shepherded: Wystan, Hild, Oswy, Tate, all of them drained back to the middle, held in place not by conviction but by the fact that you stayed near enough to hold them. The spring failed and you told them late, and they did not leave, and that is the shape of the trust they carry — not faith, but the memory of being told the truth eventually. Brand is at the dry fork still, one step afraid, one step away, the sharing you gave him sitting in him like a coal he does not know what to do with. The Red Standing One is behind you on the ridge, unchanged, waiting for the next one who climbs. You walked into the red flame and came back the colour of hesitation, and the tall one moved on, and the world aged around you into stone streets and smokestacks while you were deciding. *You kept one promise. You broke no one. The rest is what the grey took while you were learning how to speak.*

A generation on, the town around the red basin will call its fear a tradition, and the children born there will not remember it was ever a choice.

who.name: Tate
who.private: Tate was the first to see the tall one, three nights ago, and was not believed.

final.camp: the dry fork below the ridge

stories.telling: Tate was the child nobody claimed, and the flame was red before they ever reached it. They walked toward the tall one once, at dusk, and could not close the distance — the road between them was not a road yet, only ground. They ran from it later, and then ran toward Ila, and neither running amounted to anything held. At the last watch they were still moving, tentative and afraid, in a world that had grown into stone streets and smokestacks while they slept. They did not break. That is the whole of it.
stories.epilogue:
Tate, who the child nobody claims, stood at the fourth dawn in tentative fear — not broken, not converted, not still. That is what running twice will leave you: present, and uncertain, and alive in a way that costs something to name. Ila drifted back to grey, and her small trust in you was the only thing that came close to a thread between you, and it was not enough to hold her. Wystan, Brand, Hild — grey, all of them, the colour Uhtcearu leaves behind when no one fights him long enough. Oswy carried the weight of what you did not do for him, and he is grey too, but the distance between his grey and yours is measurable in the three times you were somewhere else when it mattered. One basin burns red and will not go out. The tall one is near. You are still here, which is not nothing, and is not enough.

A generation on, the clocktowers will keep time over a town that has mostly forgotten what it was afraid of, and mostly forgotten what it hoped for, and the basin on the hill will still be lit, and the children will not know what lit it, only that it has always been red.
